cf.title: Skip prefetch for block references that follow a FPW or WILL_INIT of the same block

input.subject: Skip prefetch for block references that follow a FPW or WILL_INIT of the same block

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The problem is stated with measurements, the thread shows demand from several independent people, and the change reuses the existing recent-blocks window in one file. Prefetch is advice only, so a skipped prefetch cannot change replay results. The open points are scope decisions for a committer: back-patching, v3 versus the hash-table variant, and the planned prefetcher rework.

brief.title: Skip WAL prefetch for blocks already seen with FPW or WILL_INIT
brief.problem: During recovery, the WAL prefetcher issues posix_fadvise for a block whose earlier record in the look-ahead window carried a full page image or BKPBLOCK_WILL_INIT, so replay overwrites the page anyway. Each such call can cost a real 8 KiB read. Standbys and crash recovery with recovery_prefetch enabled pay this, and the cost is highest on IOPS-limited cloud volumes.
brief.proposed_design: The patch moves the recent-blocks bookkeeping into a helper, XLogPrefetcherAddRecent(), and calls it on the FPW and WILL_INIT skip paths in XLogPrefetcherNextBlock(). The existing duplicate check then suppresses later references to the same block and counts them as skip_rep. The window size, XLOGPREFETCHER_SEQ_WINDOW_SIZE, stays unchanged.
user_visible_surface: pg_stat_recovery_prefetch counters change: fewer prefetch, more skip_rep for the same WAL.
author_claims: On NVMe, replay of 10 GB of insert-only WAL took about 31% less time, with about 90% fewer fadvise calls.
On a disk with about 2 ms latency, the same replay was about 3.1 times faster.
The fix may not help when a table has more than four indexes, because the window holds only a few blocks.
A larger window or a hash table could remove more prefetches but costs CPU; the author leaves that for a separate patch.
brief.thread_state: Ethan Mertz marked it Ready for Committer and Ashutosh Sharma posted v3; Bharath Rupireddy and Valeriy Degtyarev asked for a back-patch, and Bharath posted a hash-table variant for HEAD. Thomas Munro is studying the reports and an alternative idea, while others note that fadvise disables kernel read-ahead, which this patch does not address.
unclear: The patch does not say whether it suits back-patching, or what the risk is in stable branches.
No test case or regression test is mentioned for the new skip behaviour.
There are no measurements of workloads with many indexes, where v3 left most prefetches in place in Bharath's tests.
The thread does not settle whether the hash-table approach should replace v3 or follow it.
The thread does not say how this fix fits with Thomas Munro's planned AIO or read_stream rework of the prefetcher.

prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 reverted the whole recovery prefetch feature before release because of late-cycle bugs and missing tests. This patch is a small change to the duplicate-detection window of the feature that went in later, and it does not change replay results.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The patch changes which blocks the recovery prefetcher sends to posix_fadvise during standby replay and crash recovery.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Two participants asked for a back-patch, and the patch does not state the risk for stable branches.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch adds recent-blocks bookkeeping on the FPW and WILL_INIT skip paths of XLogPrefetcherNextBlock(), which runs for every block reference in replay.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Is the patch meant for back-patching, and what is the risk in stable branches if pg_stat_recovery_prefetch counts shift from prefetch to skip_rep?
What does v3 gain on a table with more than four indexes, where the window of XLOGPREFETCHER_SEQ_WINDOW_SIZE blocks left most prefetches in place?
Should the hash-table variant for HEAD replace v3 or follow it, and what replay CPU cost does it add?
How does this change fit with the planned AIO or read_stream rework of the prefetcher: does it survive that rework or only cover the releases before it?

committability.owner_note: Thomas Munro, who knows xlogprefetcher.c, takes part in the thread and is studying the reports and an alternative idea.
committability.liability: The owner signs for replay performance on standbys and in crash recovery, in every branch that receives the change. The code is small, and a later prefetcher rework may replace it.
committability.author_follow_up: The author rebased the patch in message #2. The brief says another contributor posted v3, so it is not shown whether the author is still active.

priority.reason: The patch is under 4 KiB in one file and adds no user-visible surface beyond shifted counter values. The thread reports a production standby problem and several independent reproductions, and the author measured about 31% less replay time on NVMe.

provisional_note: Only 3 of 17 messages and the prose of v1 and v2 were read; v3 and the hash-table variant were not seen. The back-patch risk and the CPU cost of the added bookkeeping in replay cannot be judged without the code.

precedents_retrieved.title: I thought it would be better to add a POSIx_fadvise description for the recovery_prefetch parameter here, to distinguish it from the database functions.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The entry proposes adding a posix_fadvise description to the documentation of the recovery_prefetch parameter, to tell it apart from the database functions. It is filed on the WAL prefetch thread, where recovery looks ahead in the WAL and calls PrefetchBuffer() for referenced blocks.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. They cover the WAL prefetch patch itself and a buildfarm failure that was traced to pg_walinspect, but none of them discuss the documentation change or its withdrawal.

precedents_retrieved.title: I thought it would be better to add a POSIx_fadvise description for the recovery_prefetch parameter here, to distinguish it from the database functions.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The entry proposes adding a description of posix_fadvise to the documentation of the recovery_prefetch parameter, to set it apart from database functions. It is attached to the WAL prefetch thread, where recovery reads ahead in the WAL and calls PrefetchBuffer() for referenced blocks, which relies on POSIX_FADV_WILLNEED.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. None of the shown messages discusses the documentation change. The last messages cover a buildfarm failure on topminnow, which Thomas Munro traced to pg_walinspect rather than to the prefetch code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Index Insert Prefetching
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an index AM callback amprefetch, implemented for btree, that walks the inner pages of each index and prefetches the target leaf page before index tuples are inserted. The executor calls it for all indexes, and for whole COPY batches, behind a GUC enable_insert_prefetch.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas objected that the patch duplicates the btree descent code and its runtime work, and only helps index insertion. He suggested a general async execution model, where aminsert() returns a future that can wait on I/O. The author found the idea interesting but raised open questions about control flow and concurrency. The patch then stopped applying, and no new version appears before the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't like this approach. It duplicates the tree-descend code, and it
also duplicates the work of descending the tree at runtime.

precedents_retrieved.title: prefetching for nestloop / indexscan
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an ExecPrefetch executor callback so that a nested loop reads a batch of outer rows and asks a parameterized inner index scan to prefetch the matching heap pages. It is a small proof of concept limited to nestloop with an inner index scan, controlled by a new enable_nestloop_prefetch setting.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the entry because the patch was a quick experiment and he had no time to keep working on it. Before that, Andres Freund questioned the extra executor tree traversals and suggested passing multiple values down in one parameter, possibly as one ScalarArrayOps index scan. Peter Geoghegan supported that direction. The author agreed it looks like block nested loop join, which moves the work away from this design, and his cached-data benchmark showed about a 30% regression.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But
the patch was just a quick & dirty experiment, I don't have time to work
on this right now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Adding linux cachestat in file Readv and Prefetch
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch uses the Linux 6.5 cachestat() syscall in file reads and prefetch to collect page cache statistics for a file range. It also stops prefetching when recently evicted pages suggest memory pressure.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra doubted that per-file cachestat data from one 1GB segment detects memory pressure, and he disagreed that prefetching should stop under memory pressure. He also noted that the patch had no performance evaluation. Robert Haas agreed and said pg_prewarm should read what the user asks for, and the thread does not show why the feature is needed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm not sure I even agree with the idea that we should stop prefetching
when there is memory pressure. IMHO it's perfectly fine to keep
prefetching stuff even if it triggers eviction of unnecessary pages from
page cache.

precedents_retrieved.title: Prefetch the next tuple's memory during seqscans
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_prefetch_mem() macro and uses it in heapam.c to prefetch the next tuple's memory during page-mode sequential scans. Tuples sit in reverse order on the heap page, and the author expected CPU hardware prefetchers to miss this backward access pattern.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch. After the heapgettup()/heapgettup_pagemode refactor, he could no longer show the earlier seqscan speedup, and Apple M1 and Power8 tests showed no gain. He also came to believe that modern hardware prefetchers detect backward access patterns, and he wants to benchmark this before resubmitting.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The problem I'm facing is that after Melanie's recent
refactor work done around heapgettup() [1], I can no longer get the
same speedup as before with the pg_prefetch_mem().

precedents_retrieved.title: Use fadvise in wal replay
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the startup process call posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_WILLNEED) on WAL segment files during replay, prefetching a fixed 128kB chunk ahead of the current read position. It targets standbys where OS readahead is disabled and the startup process spends its time waiting on WAL reads from disk.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks by Tomas Vondra showed the patch helps only when OS readahead is disabled, and he saw no good reason to run that way. Andres Freund added that systems without useful readahead also lack posix_fadvise, and a hardcoded 128kB distance is too short for cases such as cloud storage. The CFM marked it Returned with feedback and suggested starting over with a different approach.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It's not going to help OSs
without useful readahead, because those don't have posix_fadvise either. And
hardcoded readahead distance isn't useful - on e.g. cloud storage 128kB won't
be long enough to overcome network latency.

precedents_retrieved.title: Start WAL streaming as early as possible, without waiting for startup process to finish replaying existing WAL. This helps synchronous replication to resume quickly when significant replay lag has been built up.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch starts the WAL receiver on a standby before the startup process finishes replaying WAL already in pg_wal, so synchronous commits on the primary are not held up by replay lag. A GUC, wal_receiver_start_condition, picks when the receiver starts, and the start LSN is the beginning of the most recently flushed segment, found by reading the first page of each segment in pg_wal.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected that the start LSN is roughly the consistency point, so streaming begins too early when many local segments, often copied by hand, are still left to replay. He also rejected the WAL page checks as hard to maintain, noted that the patch requests streaming when PrimaryConnInfo is not set, and suggested a WAL reader scan from the redo point to find the real end of local WAL. The entry stayed "Waiting on Author" after this review and was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Your patch would cause streaming to begin too early, and a manual copy of segments is not a rare thing as in some environments a bulk copy of segments can make the catchup of a standby faster than streaming.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
precedents_retrieved.authors: Michael Paquier, Alexander Korotkov, Simon Riggs
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recent changes related to handling of 2PC files at recovery
Reverted commit(s): Fix handling of orphaned 2PC files in the future at recovery; Fix failures with incorrect epoch handling for 2PC files at recovery; Make use FullTransactionId in 2PC filenames; Speedup 2PC recovery by skipping two phase state files in normal path
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 8f67f994e8ea (down to v13) and c3de0f9eed38 (down to
v17), as these are proving to not be completely correct regarding two
aspects:
- In v17 and newer branches, c3de0f9eed38's check for epoch handling is
incorrect, and does not correctly handle frozen epochs.  A logic closer
to widen_snapshot_xid() should be used.  The 2PC code should try to
integrate deeper with FullTransactionIds, 5a1dfde8334b being not enough.
- In v13 and newer branches, 8f67f994e8ea is a workaround for the real
issue, which is that we should not attempt CLOG lookups without reaching
consistency.  This exists since 728bd991c3c4, and this is reachable with
ProcessTwoPhaseBuffer() called by restoreTwoPhaseData() at the beginning
of recovery.

Per discussion with Noah Misch.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent rejected this idea. P8 prefetched WAL segment files, not data blocks, and P1's revert reason (late-cycle bugs, missing tests) is about the original feature, so neither applies here. The thread mentions two earlier discussions, a March 2025 report of the same behaviour (message #4) and a 2021 hash-table discussion (message #7), but gives no rejection reason for either.

From the standards and compatibility angle there is nothing to object to. The patch adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object or dump state, and replay results do not change. The only visible change is that pg_stat_recovery_prefetch counts some blocks as skip_rep instead of prefetch, which still fits that counter's documented meaning as a repeated block, even in a back-patch. The open questions about back-patch risk and kernel read-ahead belong to other angles.

The patch changes only in-memory bookkeeping in xlogprefetcher.c. WAL format, on-disk files, catalogs, the wire protocol and struct layouts all stay the same, so there is nothing to carry across pg_upgrade or between primary and standby. Prefetch is only advice: when a later reference skips prefetch, replay still reads the block normally, so no recovery invariant depends on the change. The only visible effect is that pg_stat_recovery_prefetch counts differ, and those counters are not persistent. Back-patching raises no ABI or replication-compatibility concern from this angle.

The patch only changes which blocks the recovery prefetcher sends to posix_fadvise inside the startup process. It adds no privilege, role, GUC, SQL surface, view column or authentication path, so no new exposure to a non-superuser. The only visible change is counter values in pg_stat_recovery_prefetch, which already exist.

From the maintenance and fit angle the patch is a small, local change to one file. It adds bookkeeping only on paths that already skip a prefetch and uses the existing recent-blocks window, so it adds no API, GUC or hot-path cost for users who do not use recovery prefetch. Committability: Thomas Munro, who knows xlogprefetcher.c, is engaged in message #17 and plans an AIO rework, so v3 may be short-lived code, but it is cheap to carry. Two points could not be checked without the code: the back-patch risk in stable branches, and the absence of a regression test for the new skip path. Neither supports a level 1-2 objection on its own.

The only existing alternative is recovery_prefetch = off, and it does not do the same job: it also drops useful prefetches, as cases 7 and 8 in message #7 and the report in message #4 show. The patch extends the existing recent-blocks window instead of adding a second mechanism, and no extension or hook covers recovery prefetch.

The material shows real demand: a production outage report with numbers on a remote_apply standby (message #4), an independent earlier report cited there, and reproductions by several independent people (messages #6, #7, #13). The cost falls on the recovery path only, and the default recovery_prefetch = try exposes many users.
